The AI value chain just shifted from software differentiation to silicon ownership.

OpenAI and Broadcom unveiled a custom LLM-optimized inference chip this week — a deliberate move by the leading model provider to vertically integrate into hardware purpose-built for serving AI at scale.

For CTOs and infrastructure leaders, this is a structural signal. When the company that defines the frontier in AI models decides it needs its own silicon to serve them, it means off-the-shelf GPU infrastructure is hitting cost and efficiency ceilings that matter at scale. Inference — the cost of actually running models in production — is where the economics of AI deployment are won or lost. Custom chips designed specifically for transformer inference can dramatically change the unit economics of every AI-powered product.

For enterprises, this accelerates a coming bifurcation. Companies building on OpenAI's platform may gain access to lower inference costs over time. Companies building on competing stacks need to evaluate whether their infrastructure partners are making equivalent investments, or whether they are locked into a cost structure that becomes uncompetitive.

The AI industry is entering its infrastructure era. The winners will not just have the best models — they will have the best economics for deploying them.
